lead: Paul holds up the poor churches of Macedonia, who in their poverty begged to give, and he grounds their generosity in Christ, who “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor”. In Mark, the disciples cry out in a storm while Jesus sleeps in the stern, and he stills the wind and the sea with a word. Both readings ask where our security lies: not in what we hold, nor in calm water, but in the Lord who gave himself and who is in the boat with us.

set: For several years Paul organised a collection among his Gentile churches for the poor among the believers in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–27; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4; Galatians 2:10). For him it was more than relief: it was a sign that Jews and Gentiles who believed in Christ were one Church.

The Corinthians had begun the collection a year earlier and then let it slip. Paul does not command; he tells them what the churches of Macedonia, Philippi, Thessalonica and Beroea among them, have done, and points them to Christ.
str: vv. 1–5: the example of Macedonia: affliction, poverty, joy, and generosity beyond their means.
v. 6: Titus is sent to complete the work in Corinth.
vv. 7–8: excel in this as in everything; not a command, but a test of love.
v. 9: the reason: the self-giving of Christ.
vv. 10–11: finish what you began, according to your means.
kw: The key word of the chapter. The NRSV gives it as “grace” (v. 1), “privilege” (v. 4), “generous undertaking” (vv. 6–7) and “generous act” (v. 9). Paul calls the collection itself a grace: giving is first something God gives.
Fellowship, communion, partnership. The Macedonians beg for a share in the service of the saints. The same word describes the life of the first community in Acts 2:42.
The verb means to become a beggar, to be reduced to poverty. Paul is speaking of the whole self-emptying of the Son, from the Incarnation to the Cross (compare Philippians 2:6–8).
vv: their abundant joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.
Joy and poverty together produce generosity. Generosity does not depend on having much.
they gave themselves first to the Lord and, by the will of God, to us,
The order matters. A gift of money that does not come from a gift of self is not yet what Paul is asking for.
though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich.
The whole Gospel in one sentence. Christian giving is a share in this exchange.
now finish doing it, so that your eagerness may be matched by completing it according to your means.
Good intentions are not enough. Paul asks for what is possible, “according to your means”, but asks that it be done.
ch: The Catechism links the collection made at the Holy Qurbana with this very verse: from the beginning Christians brought, with the bread and wine, gifts to share with those in need, following the example of Christ who became poor to make us rich (CCC 1351). It cites St Justin's description of the Sunday gathering in the second century, where those who have means give what they wish, and the one who presides helps orphans, widows and all in need (First Apology 67).

r.h: Even the wind and the sea obey him
set: The same day Jesus taught in parables from the boat (4:1), he tells his disciples to cross the Sea of Galilee to the other side, the region of the Gerasenes (5:1), largely Gentile country. The lake lies far below sea level among hills, and sudden violent winds are well known there.

For Israel the sea was a picture of chaos, which only God can master (Psalm 89:9; Psalm 107:23–30). Jonah too slept in a ship in a storm (Jonah 1:5). Mark's account invites the question with which it ends: who then is this?
str: vv. 35–36: evening; they set out, taking him “just as he was”.
v. 38: Jesus asleep; the disciples' cry.
v. 39: the rebuke and the calm.
vv. 40–41: Jesus' question about faith; their question about him.
kw: The same verb Mark used when Jesus rebuked an unclean spirit in the synagogue at Capernaum (1:25). Jesus speaks to the storm as to a hostile power.
Literally “be muzzled”. It is the same verb as “Be silent!” spoken to the unclean spirit (1:25).
they were filled with great awe
Literally “they feared a great fear”. Their fear of the storm becomes the awe of people who stand before God at work.
vv: But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion;
Only Mark mentions the cushion. The detail sounds like an eyewitness memory. His sleep is the sleep of trust (Psalm 4:8).
Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?
It is the cry of many believers in many storms. The Lord does not rebuke them for crying out, only for being afraid.
“Peace! Be still!” Then the wind ceased, and there was a dead calm.
Why are you afraid? Have you still no faith?
Faith here is not the absence of storms, but trust in the One who is in the boat.
Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?
The disciples answer without knowing it: only the Lord commands the sea (Psalm 107:29).
ch: Tertullian saw the little boat as a figure of the Church, tossed by the waves of the world while the Lord seems to sleep (On Baptism 12, in substance). St Augustine applied the scene to each heart: when we are insulted and the waves rise, it is because Christ is asleep in us, that is, our faith has fallen asleep; wake him, and the storm is calmed (in substance). Pope Francis meditated on this passage during the pandemic, on 27 March 2020, in an empty St Peter's Square, reminding the world that we are all in the same boat.

study: The Macedonians “gave themselves first to the Lord”. What would it look like for my family to give ourselves first, and then our gifts?
What storm am I in at present, and how can I let the Lord's question, “Why are you afraid?”, become an invitation to trust?
